title: Trump Media plans paid fast access to Truth Social posts for Wall Street firms
description_medium: Trump Media discussed charging financial firms up to $100,000 a month for a faster feed of Truth Social posts, including posts by President Donald Trump, according to reporting in July 2026. The Associated Press described the planned service as offering traders an earlier look at posts that can move markets. The linked report does not establish a separate service providing advance notice of foreign-policy decisions or show that the policy itself was disclosed privately before a public post.
description_long: In July 2026, Trump Media & Technology Group discussed selling Wall Street firms faster access to posts on Truth Social, including posts by President Donald Trump. The Associated Press reported that the planned service would offer traders a “sneak peek” at posts before they appeared to the broader public; Reuters separately reported that firms could be charged as much as $100,000 per month for the fastest feed. The company’s pitch raised questions about whether a sitting president’s media business could profit from market-moving communications posted on a platform he owned and used for policy announcements. This was a proposal and launch plan at the time of the early coverage, not evidence that financial firms received confidential advance notice of government decisions before Trump chose to announce them. The linked AP story describes paid access to social-media content and potential ethical and trading concerns. It does not support the assigned headline’s claim that the administration sold foreign-policy advance notice, nor does it establish insider trading or prove that a subscriber made a specific profit. Later reports about the service’s August launch and subscriber agreements describe subsequent developments and should be treated separately from the initial proposal.
evidence_notes: AP coverage describes planned paid fast access/sneak peeks to posts; Reuters reports proposed price range. The link does not document private foreign-policy briefings.
corrected_wording: Replace claim of administration selling advance foreign-policy notice with the more limited proposed paid access to Truth Social posts, including presidential posts.

title: Lawmakers seek Pentagon watchdog review of companies backed by Trump’s sons
description_medium: After The Washington Post reported that 15 companies backed by Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump had received $3.2 billion in federal contracts, loans and investments, Democratic lawmakers asked the Defense Department inspector general to investigate. The Post’s total combines different forms of federal support, not just Pentagon contracts. One example was a $620 million Pentagon loan to rare-earth magnet maker Vulcan Elements, in which Trump Jr. had invested. The request is not an inspector general finding of wrongdoing.
description_long: The Washington Post reported in July and August 2026 that 15 companies with investments from Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump had received a combined $3.2 billion in federal contracts, loans and investments. Much of the reported support came after their father returned to office, though the total included different types of assistance across government and should not be described as $3.2 billion in Pentagon contracts alone. One prominent example was a $620 million loan from the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet manufacturer in which Donald Trump Jr. had invested. In response to the reporting, Democratic lawmakers asked the Defense Department inspector general to investigate the awards and potential conflicts of interest. The Post also noted that several companies had received government business before the sons invested, a relevant qualification when assessing whether their connections influenced awards. The event is the lawmakers’ request for oversight following the newspaper’s investigation. The assigned reporting does not include an inspector general conclusion, and the amounts alone do not establish that any contract or loan was awarded improperly. A company-by-company review and the watchdog’s findings would be needed to resolve those questions.
evidence_notes: Washington Post investigation reports 15 companies, $3.2bn in combined contracts/investments/loans, and $620m Vulcan Elements Pentagon loan; follow-up reports lawmakers' IG request. It notes some pre-existing federal contracts.
corrected_wording: Separate the $3.2bn aggregate from Pentagon-only awards and describe the IG inquiry as a request, not a finding. Attribute conflict concerns.

title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza roadmap while Hamas says it remains committed
description_medium: On August 9, 2026, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel rejected a 15-point U.S.-backed Gaza roadmap and would not withdraw its forces until Hamas was disarmed. Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said the group remained committed to the roadmap and expected mediators and the United States to press Israel. The competing statements left the proposed next phase of the ceasefire uncertain; they did not establish that the plan had been fully accepted or implemented by all parties.
description_long: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on August 9, 2026, that Israel rejected the 15-point Gaza roadmap advanced by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace and would not withdraw Israeli forces until Hamas was “genuinely disarmed.” The plan was meant to move a prior ceasefire framework toward phased disarmament, Israeli withdrawal and a transition to Palestinian civilian administration. Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said the group remained committed to the roadmap and expected the United States and mediators to pressure Netanyahu. That statement followed the Board of Peace’s July announcement that Hamas and other factions had agreed to the plan, although Hamas’s position tied disarmament to Israel meeting its ceasefire commitments and withdrawing. The public disagreement exposed a gap between the parties over sequencing and conditions. It left the proposed next phase uncertain; it did not constitute an implemented agreement or demonstrate that either side had accepted every provision without conditions. The AP report described Netanyahu’s rejection and Hamas’s stated commitment, while the broader terms appear in U.S. and other reporting. The supplied source does not establish whether negotiations later resolved those differences or whether the roadmap produced a withdrawal.
evidence_notes: AP Aug. 9 report gives Netanyahu's rejection and Hamas official Bassem Naim's response. White House statement and Reuters explainer detail the roadmap and conditional nature of positions.
corrected_wording: Use “remained committed” rather than unqualified acceptance; clarify Israel rejected the document and no implementation agreement is shown.

title: U.S. announces separate tariff measures against Canada and Brazil
description_medium: In July 2026, the Trump administration announced different tariff actions involving Canada and Brazil. On July 16, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed a 25% tariff on certain Brazilian goods under a Section 301 investigation covering issues such as digital trade, preferential tariffs, intellectual property, ethanol access and deforestation. On July 20, President Trump announced 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian products, citing Canada’s treatment of U.S. cars, alcohol and dairy. The measures were separate actions with different legal bases and stated rationales.
description_long: The Trump administration announced two distinct tariff actions in July 2026, rather than one joint tariff package. On July 16, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed a 25% tariff on certain Brazilian goods under Section 301 of the Trade Act. The investigation addressed issues including digital trade and electronic payments, preferential tariff treatment, intellectual property, ethanol market access and deforestation; the Brazilian government rejected the action. Four days later, Trump announced 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian products, with the administration citing Canada’s treatment of U.S. car, alcohol and dairy producers. Reuters reported that the Canadian levies were scheduled to take effect August 19 and included exemptions for some categories such as energy, fish, potash and critical minerals. The actions therefore involved different countries, legal authorities and stated grounds. They formed part of the administration’s wider use of tariffs in trade policy, but should not be presented as a single coordinated measure or as a finding that either country violated the law. The available reports describe the announced rates and rationale, not their ultimate economic effects or the outcome of later negotiations.
evidence_notes: Reuters and USTR report Canada's July 20 announcement/50% rate and Brazil's separate July 16 Section 301 action/25% rate, with distinct grounds.
corrected_wording: Separate the Canada and Brazil measures by date, rate, statute and stated grounds; avoid presenting them as one tariff package.

title: Trump weighs declaring victory if Strait of Hormuz reopens, without a nuclear deal
description_medium: In August 2026, reporting citing people familiar with administration deliberations said Donald Trump was considering declaring the Iran campaign a success if the Strait of Hormuz reopened, even without a nuclear agreement. Reopening the shipping lane was a central point in negotiations, and Iran’s nuclear program remained unresolved. The account described a possible political framing, not a final presidential decision or an end to the conflict. It did not establish that Tehran had agreed to reopen the strait.
description_long: A Wall Street Journal report in August 2026 said President Donald Trump was weighing whether to declare victory in the conflict with Iran if the Strait of Hormuz reopened, even without securing a nuclear agreement. The strategic waterway had been a central point of dispute and a priority in negotiations, while the status of Iran’s nuclear program remained unsettled. The possible declaration would represent a public description of the campaign’s outcome; it would not itself prove that U.S. objectives had been achieved or that hostilities had ended. Contemporary reporting said the option was under consideration, not that Trump had made a final decision to accept it. The article also described disagreement within the administration over whether a reopened strait without nuclear concessions would constitute success. The report therefore captures a debate over how to define an acceptable outcome and communicate it to the public. It does not establish that Iran had agreed to reopen the waterway, that the United States had secured a nuclear commitment, or that Trump ultimately announced victory on those terms. Those later developments require separate reporting.
evidence_notes: Haaretz report attributes the contemplated victory declaration to WSJ reporting. AP linked page was inaccessible in this review; it is retained as the assigned source reference.
corrected_wording: Frame the declaration as an option under consideration and distinguish reopening Hormuz from a nuclear deal or actual end to hostilities.

title: House Democrats release Epstein emails raising questions about Trump’s knowledge
description_medium: On November 12, 2025, House Oversight Democrats released emails from Jeffrey Epstein’s estate that they said raised questions about Donald Trump’s knowledge of Epstein’s abuse. In one 2019 message, Epstein wrote that Trump “knew about the girls,” without specifying what he meant. Another email referred to Trump having spent time at Epstein’s home with an alleged victim. The emails were allegations and correspondence, not flight logs or an independent finding that Trump participated in abuse.
description_long: House Oversight Democrats released emails from Jeffrey Epstein’s estate on November 12, 2025, saying the messages raised questions about what President Donald Trump knew about Epstein’s abuse of underage girls. In a 2019 email to author Michael Wolff, Epstein wrote that Trump “knew about the girls,” but the phrase’s meaning was unclear from the message alone. Other emails discussed an alleged victim and Trump’s presence at Epstein’s home. Republicans on the committee released a separate tranche of 20,000 pages later that day, while the White House dismissed the Democrats’ interpretation. The release took place amid a congressional dispute over making government-held Epstein records public and after a newly sworn-in House member provided the final signature for a discharge petition seeking a vote on disclosure. The event was the publication of estate correspondence and ensuing political dispute. The emails do not by themselves verify Epstein’s claims, establish that Trump participated in abuse, or constitute flight logs or phone records. Those elements in the supplied draft are not substantiated by the linked Reuters report and should not be folded into this event without separate documentary sources.
evidence_notes: Reuters describes the emails and quotes Epstein's ambiguous wording; House Oversight Republicans' official release confirms the separate 20,000-page tranche. The event is email release, not flight-log publication.
corrected_wording: Replace unsupported flight log/phone record and Mark Epstein testimony claims with documented contents of the November 12 email release; attribute allegations.

title: Court filing recounts Jane Doe 102’s allegation that Maxwell approached her at Mar-a-Lago
description_medium: A 2009 court filing in litigation over Jeffrey Epstein described Jane Doe 102’s allegation that Ghislaine Maxwell approached her while she worked at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club and recruited her for Maxwell and Epstein when she was a minor. The filing also cited testimony by Epstein’s brother that Trump had flown on Epstein’s plane. These are allegations and references in a court submission, not judicial findings; the linked Reuters article concerns a later House email release and does not establish them.
description_long: A filing from 2009 litigation involving Jeffrey Epstein summarized allegations by a plaintiff identified as Jane Doe 102. It said she claimed Ghislaine Maxwell approached her while she was working at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club and recruited her, when she was a minor, to work for Maxwell and Epstein. The filing also recounted testimony by Jeffrey Epstein’s brother, Mark Epstein, that Trump had flown on Jeffrey Epstein’s plane. Those statements appear as allegations and references in a court submission; they are not judicial findings that Maxwell recruited the plaintiff at Mar-a-Lago, that the described plane travel involved abuse, or that Trump participated in trafficking. The claim about the plaintiff’s recruitment is distinct from later congressional releases of Epstein estate emails, which are the subject of the linked Reuters source in the original record. The court document is the appropriate source for the allegations described here. The record’s additional assertion that Trump banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago after a separate sexual-assault claim is not established by this filing and is omitted. Any account should preserve the pseudonym used in the litigation and distinguish the plaintiff’s allegation from proven facts.
evidence_notes: DOJ-hosted civil filing describes Doe 102's allegation and quotes testimony cited in litigation. Reuters link is a distinct email-release event and should not be used as evidence for this older allegation.
corrected_wording: Attribute the allegation to the 2009 filing and keep the 2025 email release separate. Delete unsupported Mar-a-Lago ban claim.

title: NPR finds Epstein files about a Trump assault allegation absent from public DOJ database
description_medium: An NPR investigation published February 24, 2026, found that more than 50 pages of FBI interviews and notes concerning a woman’s allegation of sexual abuse by Donald Trump when she was a minor appeared to be missing from the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database. NPR said its review of serial numbers and agency records indicated the documents had existed. The allegation is unverified, and DOJ said the unpublished material was privileged, duplicative or connected to an ongoing investigation.
description_long: NPR reported on February 24, 2026, that more than 50 pages of FBI interviews and notes related to an allegation against Donald Trump appeared to be missing from the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database. NPR compared serial numbers, interview records and other internal tracking information and found references indicating that the material existed, including interviews with a woman who accused Trump of sexually abusing her when she was a minor. The allegation itself is not proof of an assault. NPR said DOJ initially did not explain the status of the specific records; after publication, a department spokesperson said unpublished documents were privileged, duplicates or connected to an ongoing investigation. A House Oversight Democrat said the committee would pursue a parallel inquiry into the handling of the files. The White House disputed the allegation and said Trump had been exonerated. The report documented questions about completeness and disclosure of the public database, rather than establishing who made the decision to withhold records or why. The supplied claim that all files were released in March under pressure from lawsuits is not established by the NPR article and is left out. Later publication or litigation developments need separate sourcing.
evidence_notes: NPR's report, republished by member stations, documents its serial-number review, apparently missing 50+ pages, DOJ explanation after publication, and Oversight response.
corrected_wording: Describe missing public records and NPR's evidence, not a proven DOJ motive or confirmed later release; keep underlying allegation explicitly unverified.

title: IRS settlement with Trump includes broad protection from future tax claims
description_medium: A May 2026 settlement of Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS over leaked tax returns included provisions permanently dropping federal tax claims against Trump and related parties. A later addendum by Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche extended protections involving audits, examinations and claims connected to prior tax matters for Trump, family members and affiliated entities. The agreement prompted criticism and a challenge by the National Treasury Employees Union. It did not establish that Trump had committed tax wrongdoing or that every possible future audit was barred.
description_long: The federal government settled Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns in May 2026. The settlement included a provision permanently dropping tax claims against Trump. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche issued an addendum the following day that expanded protections for Trump, family members, companies and affiliated parties against audits, examinations and related tax claims involving matters covered by the agreement, including tax returns filed before its effective date. The arrangement drew scrutiny because it arose from a settlement resolving a lawsuit brought by the sitting president against his own government. The National Treasury Employees Union challenged the arrangement in court, arguing that the government had exceeded its authority and created unequal treatment. The legal challenge and public criticism do not themselves resolve whether the settlement provisions are lawful; the linked AP account describes the agreement and dispute, not a final court ruling. The word “immunity” in the original title overstates the scope if read to mean that Trump or his organization could never be audited for any future conduct. The documents concern specified claims and past tax matters covered by the settlement. The record supports describing that unusual protection and the ensuing challenge without asserting a judicial finding of corruption.
evidence_notes: AP reports settlement and Blanche addendum; DOJ settlement document details covered claims; Washington Post reports NTEU challenge. Scope is prior tax-related matters and specified claims, not blanket immunity for all future conduct.
corrected_wording: Change “audit immunity” to specific settlement protections for past and covered tax claims; attribute the NTEU's legal challenge and avoid asserting unlawfulness as adjudicated.

title: Trump Media launches paid Truth API for faster access to posts, charging firms up to $100,000 monthly
description_medium: Trump Media launched Truth API on August 1, 2026, offering paying customers faster access to posts on Truth Social, including President Donald Trump’s. The company said high-frequency trading firms were among its early customers and reported monthly fees ranging from about $60,000 to $100,000. The service delivers posts as they are published through a fast data feed; reports do not establish that five firms front-ran presidential announcements or that courts or regulators found insider trading.
description_long: Trump Media & Technology Group launched Truth API on August 1, 2026, as a paid feed that gives subscribers faster access to posts on Truth Social, including posts by President Donald Trump. The company said it had signed agreements with more than ten customers in the first weeks after launch, most of them high-frequency trading firms, and that fees generally ranged from $60,000 to $100,000 a month. The service raised ethical and legal questions because Trump’s posts can move financial markets and the company is partly owned by the president. The earlier proposal had been described as a way to give customers a “sneak peek” at posts; reporting about the launched product says it provided fast access to posts as they were published, not a documented private briefing about policy decisions before Trump posted them publicly. Media and press-freedom organizations later sued, arguing the paid service created unequal access to presidential communications. Critics have called the practice insider trading, but the existence of a paid feed does not establish that a subscriber traded unlawfully or that regulators made such a finding. The record should distinguish launch and subscription pricing from claims about market manipulation or subscriber profits.
evidence_notes: CNN report says signed contracts and up to $100k/month; Guardian reports Aug. 1 rollout and later lawsuit. Sources don't say five firms front-ran trades or establish insider trading.
corrected_wording: Distinguish faster access to published posts from advance notice of private policy decisions; attribute legal/ethical criticism without asserting a legal finding.
